title: Why and when Budd took up the soprano saxophone
summary: Hinton praises Budd's in-tune soprano; Budd explains the horn's history and that his wife persuaded him to switch from clarinet.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Now I'd just like to say this, Budd, ask you this -- you're recognized as the greatest living

soprano saxophone player alive. I've heard you in Jimmy Weston's, and I've heard you play in my dear buddy -- I've heard you play in -- being a bass player, I don't know too much about the instrument because I don't know anything about a saxophone, but you're one of the few men that can play beautifully in tune. I'm talking about the straight soprano saxophone.
Now it seems to me that -- I don't know if you were playing it back in those days. Now when did you start playing it and why?

Well, I did play it years ago, I think, when it was first invented. I'm using the word first invented because I had never heard of it before, and that must have been back around 1927 or eight when I first bought a soprano. And it was invented to emulate the woman soprano voice. That's why it was named soprano saxophone. And when I play the soprano saxophone I try to do just that. That's why I use the vibrato, and I try to play it just as someone would be singing a beautiful ballad, and this is the way I try to play it.

So then they used to call them fish horns, like the eel, see? The long horn. But then it seems that when you ever put three or four of them together, they sound horrible. Well, back in those days Frank Skinner and all of them were writing arrangements for the soprano saxophone, but they could

never seem to get a bunch of them that could play these cats in tune together. So like they sort of went out of style because they sound kind of bad when you put three or four of them together. Then I didn't take it up again until -- but I always had one, and I started to fool around with it, and my wife heard it, and she says, gee, that sounds beautiful. Why don't you play that instrument? I believe that you could do something with that instrument.

So I said, well, I think I will give it a try; instead of continuing with the clarinet, I think I'll just pick up soprano, and of course I was inspired by the master, Sidney Bechet. And I was his understudy once in a play.
